title: Lists
summary: A List<T> is an array that grows: add, insert, remove, search and sort without counting slots.

steps.title: An array that grows
body: An array's size is fixed the moment you create it. That is awkward when you do not know how many items are coming: lines the user types, matches found in a search.
A **`List<T>`** grows as you add to it. The `T` is the type of the items, written in angle brackets.
```csharp
var names = new List<string>();
names.Add("Ann");
names.Add("Bo");
Console.WriteLine(names.Count);  // 2
Console.WriteLine(names[0]);     // Ann
names[1] = "Bob";               // replace an item
foreach (string name in names)
Console.WriteLine(name);
- `Add` puts an item on the end.
- Indexing with `[ ]` works exactly as it does for arrays, starting at 0.
- A list has a **`Count`** where an array has a `Length`.
You can also start with some items: `var primes = new List<int> { 2, 3, 5 };`

steps.prompt: Complete the program so it creates an empty list of strings, adds one item, and prints how many items there are.
steps.explain: `List<string>` is the type, `Add` appends, and a list's size is its `Count`. `Length` belongs to arrays and strings.

steps.title: Keep the evens
prompt: Write a method `List<int> Evens(int[] numbers)` that returns a list of the even numbers from the array, in their original order.
You cannot know in advance how many there will be. That is exactly the job a list is for.
starter: // add each even number to result
template: Dojo.Eq("Evens of { 1, 2, 3, 4 } is [2, 4]", new List<int> { 2, 4 }, Evens(new[] { 1, 2, 3, 4 }));
Dojo.Eq("Evens of { 1, 3, 5 } is empty", new List<int>(), Evens(new[] { 1, 3, 5 }));
Dojo.Eq("Evens of an empty array is empty", new List<int>(), Evens(new int[0]));
hints: Walk the array with `foreach (int n in numbers)`.

steps.title: Changing a list
body: A list can do much more than grow at the end.
```csharp
var nums = new List<int> { 5, 3, 8 };
nums.Insert(1, 9);    // 5, 9, 3, 8   put 9 at index 1, the rest shift right
nums.Remove(3);       // 5, 9, 8      remove the first item equal to 3
nums.RemoveAt(0);     // 9, 8         remove whatever is at index 0
nums.Sort();          // 8, 9         smallest first
Console.WriteLine(nums.Contains(9));   // True
Watch the difference: `Remove` takes a **value** to look for, `RemoveAt` takes a **position**. `Remove` returns `false` when the value is not there, and changes nothing.
`Sort` puts numbers in ascending order and strings in alphabetical order.

> **Tip:** do not add or remove items inside a `foreach` over the same list. The loop loses its place and the program crashes with an `InvalidOperationException`. Use a `for` loop that counts **backwards**: removing an item then only moves items you have already visited.

steps.explain: The list goes `a b`, then `a b c`, then `z a b c`, then `z a c`. That is three items, and index 1 holds `a`.

steps.prompt: A list starts as `5, 3, 8` each time. Match each call to the list it leaves behind.
Arrange the lines so the program adds `milk`, then adds `eggs` only if it is not already in the cart, and finally prints `eggs`.
steps.explain: `milk` must go in first so that `eggs` lands at index 1. Checking `Contains` before `Add` is the simple way to keep a list free of duplicates.

steps.prompt: A program reads numbers from the user until they type `done`. You cannot know how many there will be. What should hold them?
options: A `List<int>`, adding each number as it arrives
An `int[]` with 1000 slots, to be safe
steps.explain: An array needs its size up front. Guess too low and it overflows, guess too high and most of it is empty slots you must remember to ignore. A list is always exactly as big as what you put in.

items: Its size is fixed once created

steps.title: The vanishing negatives
prompt: `RemoveNegatives` should delete every number below zero from the list it is given. `3, -1, 4, -5` should become `3, 4`.
It crashes as soon as it removes something. Run it, read the error, and rewrite the loop so it is safe.
template: Dojo.Try("RemoveNegatives on [3, -1, 4, -5] does not crash", () => { var a = new List<int> { 3, -1, 4, -5 }; RemoveNegatives(a); Dojo.Eq("[3, -1, 4, -5] becomes [3, 4]", new List<int> { 3, 4 }, a); });
Dojo.Try("RemoveNegatives on [-1, -2, -3, 6] does not crash", () => { var b = new List<int> { -1, -2, -3, 6 }; RemoveNegatives(b); Dojo.Eq("[-1, -2, -3, 6] becomes [6]", new List<int> { 6 }, b); });
Dojo.Try("RemoveNegatives on [-7, -7] does not crash", () => { var c = new List<int> { -7, -7 }; RemoveNegatives(c); Dojo.Eq("[-7, -7] becomes empty", new List<int>(), c); });
Dojo.Try("RemoveNegatives on [1, 0, 2] does not crash", () => { var d = new List<int> { 1, 0, 2 }; RemoveNegatives(d); Dojo.Eq("[1, 0, 2] is unchanged", new List<int> { 1, 0, 2 }, d); });
hints: A `foreach` does not allow the list to change while it is running. Switch to a `for` loop with an index.
Count **backwards**, from `numbers.Count - 1` down to `0`. Going forwards, each removal shifts the next item into the slot you just checked, and it gets skipped.
`for (int i = numbers.Count - 1; i >= 0; i--)` and inside it `if (numbers[i] < 0) numbers.RemoveAt(i);`

steps.title: The guest list
prompt: Read names, one per line, until the line `done`. Then print the guest list:
- each name **once**, even if it was entered several times
- followed by a line with the total
starter: // 1. read lines until "done", adding each new name
// 3. print the numbered names, then the total

tests.name: five guests
tests.stdin:
Eve
Dan
Cal
Bea
Abe
done
tests.expect:
1. Abe
2. Bea
3. Cal
4. Dan
5. Eve
Total: 5

hints: Read with `while (true)`, `break` on `"done"`, and only `Add` a name when `!names.Contains(line)`.
After the loop, `names.Sort();` puts them in alphabetical order.
You need the position for the numbering, so print with a `for` loop: `$"{i + 1}. {names[i]}"`. The total is `names.Count`.
